def: A group of words established by usage as having a meaning not deducible from the individual words.
ex: Learning common English idioms will make your everyday conversations sound much more natural.
nat: He translated the idiom literally, which confused everyone in the room.

mis.bad: How many idioms do you speak?
mis.good: How many languages do you speak?
mis.why: In English, "idiom" means an idiomatic expression, not a whole spoken language ("language").

def: To catch fire or cause to catch fire, or arouse strong feelings.
ex: A tiny spark from the faulty socket ignited dry paper on the desk.
nat: The controversial decision ignited protests across several major cities.

mis.bad: The discussion ignited about the budget.
mis.good: The discussion ignited a debate on the budget.
mis.why: "Ignite" is transitive; do not insert "about" immediately after it.

def: Lack of knowledge or information.
ex: His complete ignorance of basic tax law caused serious problems for the startup.
nat: Ignorance of the law is no excuse in modern court proceedings.

mis.bad: He has an ignorance about finances.
mis.good: He has a lack of knowledge / showed ignorance of finances.
mis.why: Use "ignorance of" a subject, not "an ignorance about".

def: Unable to read or write, or lacking basic knowledge in a particular field.
ex: The charity helps functionally illiterate adults gain essential reading and computer skills.
nat: Many young workers are computer illiterate when entering technical roles.

mis.bad: He is illiterate with computer tools.
mis.good: He is digitally illiterate / illiterate in computers.
mis.why: Use "digitally illiterate" or "illiterate in [field]", not "illiterate with".

def: To light up and make visible, or explain and clarify a subject.
ex: Bright morning sunlight illuminated the quiet valley and revealed the winding river.
nat: The keynote speaker illuminated several complex aspects of generative artificial intelligence.

mis.bad: The teacher illuminated about the topic.
mis.good: The teacher illuminated the topic.
mis.why: "Illuminate" is transitive and takes a direct object without "about".

def: A deceptive appearance or impression, or a false idea or belief.
ex: High monthly salaries often create the false illusion that spending can stay unlimited.
nat: Mirrors around the small studio apartment created an illusion of extra space.

mis.bad: He had an illusion of buy a car.
mis.good: He had an illusion of buying a car / dreamt of buying a car.
mis.why: Use "under the illusion that" or use "dream/hope" instead of "have an illusion".

def: To copy someone's speech or behavior, or simulate the appearance of something.
ex: Young children naturally imitate the speech patterns and facial expressions of their parents.
nat: Cheap synthetic materials often try to imitate the soft texture of real leather.

mis.bad: He imitated to his older brother.
mis.good: He imitated his older brother.
mis.why: "Imitate" is transitive; do not place "to" before the person.

def: Extremely large or great, especially in scale or degree.
ex: Rebuilding the city after the devastating flood required an immense amount of capital.
nat: Working at the hospital gave the medical students an immense amount of satisfaction.

mis.bad: The task was of an immense difficult.
mis.good: The task was of immense difficulty / immensely difficult.
mis.why: Use the adjective "immense" to modify a noun directly: "immense difficulty".

def: About to happen, usually said of an event or danger.
ex: The dark clouds and dropping air pressure signaled an imminent thunderstorm over the coast.
nat: Engineers warned the management team about the imminent failure of the backup server.

mis.bad: His promotion is eminent.
mis.good: His promotion is imminent.
mis.why: Do not confuse "imminent" (happening soon) with "eminent" (distinguished, famous).

def: Treating all rivals or disputants equally; fair and unbiased.
ex: The committee appointed an impartial mediator to resolve the disputes between the founders.
nat: A good investigative reporter must remain strictly impartial when covering sensitive elections.

mis.bad: The judge was impartial with the company.
mis.good: The judge was impartial toward both parties.
mis.why: Say "impartial toward / between", not "impartial with".

def: Not perfect; faulty or incomplete.
ex: An imperfect plan executed immediately is often far better than a flawless plan delayed.
nat: Human memory is imperfect and changes slightly every time we recall an event.

mis.bad: My English is very imperfectly.
mis.good: My English is very imperfect.
mis.why: Use the adjective "imperfect" after the linking verb "is", not the adverb.

def: Not showing or influenced by personal feelings, or not existing as a person.
ex: Automated customer support emails often feel cold and impersonal to frustrated paying clients.
nat: Large corporations can become strangely impersonal as thousands of new employees join.

mis.bad: The message was very impersonally.
mis.good: The message was very impersonal.
mis.why: Use the adjective "impersonal" following "was", not the adverb form.

def: To make a person or area poor, or exhaust the quality or strength of something.
ex: Decades of intensive farming without crop rotation will impoverish even the richest agricultural soil.
nat: High medical debts continue to impoverish thousands of families every single year.

mis.bad: The crisis impoverished to the population.
mis.good: The crisis impoverished the population.
mis.why: "Impoverish" is a transitive verb that requires no preposition "to".

def: Not likely to happen or be true.
ex: Winning the national lottery jackpot twice is statistically improbable yet not completely impossible.
nat: The detective solved the case by exploring several highly improbable explanations first.

mis.bad: It is improbable of him to arrive.
mis.good: It is improbable that he will arrive / unlikely for him to arrive.
mis.why: Use "improbable that + clause", not "improbable of [person] to".

def: Not in accordance with accepted rules or standards, especially of morality or honesty.
ex: The auditor found improper accounting practices that had gone unnoticed for several quarters.
nat: Using administrative privileges for personal projects is completely improper in corporate security.

mis.bad: His conduct was improper with the company.
mis.good: His conduct was improper for a company officer.
mis.why: Use "improper for [a role/person]", not "improper with".

def: To create and perform music, drama, or verse without preparation, or produce something on the spot.
ex: When the projector failed during the presentation, Carlos had to improvise with whiteboards.
nat: Good jazz musicians can improvise melodic solos over unexpected chord progressions effortlessly.

mis.bad: I improvised about what to say.
mis.good: I improvised what to say.
mis.why: "Improvise" takes a direct object without "about".

def: Not resulting from or achieved through deliberate planning; accidental.
ex: An inadvertent slip of the keyboard deleted three lines of production database code.
nat: The hospital apologized sincerely for the inadvertent disclosure of private patient records.

mis.bad: The disclosure was made by inadvertent.
mis.good: The disclosure was inadvertent / made inadvertently.
mis.why: Use "inadvertent" as an adjective or "inadvertently" as an adverb, not "by inadvertent".

def: Unable to be heard.
ex: His whispered explanation was completely inaudible above the loud roar of construction machinery.
nat: Certain high ultrasonic sound frequencies are totally inaudible to normal human ears.

mis.bad: His voice was inaudible for me.
mis.good: His voice was inaudible to me.
mis.why: Say something is "inaudible to someone", not "for someone".

def: Unable to do something; lacking the ability, fitness, or quality necessary for an action.
ex: The outdated computer processor was completely incapable of running modern neural network models.
nat: After working twenty hours straight, he was utterly incapable of making sound judgments.

mis.bad: The system is incapable to process payments.
mis.good: The system is incapable of processing payments.
mis.why: Always use "incapable of + -ing", never "incapable to + base verb".

def: To provide someone with an incentive for doing something.
ex: Tech startups often incentivize early employees with attractive company stock option packages.
nat: City governments offer tax credits to incentivize homeowners to install solar energy panels.

mis.bad: We must incentivize to our staff.
mis.good: We must incentivize our staff.
mis.why: "Incentivize" takes a direct object without "to".

def: A person's natural tendency or urge to act or feel in a particular way.
ex: My immediate inclination was to refuse the dubious offer and look elsewhere.
nat: She felt an overwhelming inclination to book the ticket and embark immediately.

mis.bad: I have no inclination for study tonight.
mis.good: I have no inclination to study tonight.
mis.why: Use "inclination to + verb", not "for + base verb".

def: Including or covering all the services, facilities, or items normally expected or required.
ex: The resort package offers fully inclusive pricing covering daily meals, drinks, and airport transfers.
nat: We want to build a truly inclusive workplace where diverse ideas flourish naturally.

mis.bad: The tour is inclusive with drinks.
mis.good: The tour is inclusive of drinks / all-inclusive.
mis.why: Use "inclusive of [items]", not "inclusive with".

def: Not able to exist or work together in harmony or without conflict.
ex: The updated mobile application proved totally incompatible with older versions of the operating system.
nat: Their aggressive work styles were fundamentally incompatible, creating frequent friction during meetings.

mis.bad: This software is incompatible to my computer.
mis.good: This software is incompatible with my computer.
mis.why: Use "incompatible with", never "incompatible to".

def: Not having or showing the necessary skills to do something successfully.
ex: An incompetent contractor ruined the kitchen renovation, forcing the family to hire professionals.
nat: Senior executives were replaced after an incompetent financial audit misled outside institutional investors.

mis.bad: He was considered incompetent to driving.
mis.good: He was considered incompetent at driving / to drive.
mis.why: Use "incompetent at + -ing" or "incompetent to + base verb".

def: Not having all the necessary or appropriate parts.
ex: The loan application was rejected immediately because several financial disclosures remained incomplete.
nat: Our team had to postpone the rollout because user testing was still incomplete.

mis.bad: The report was in incomplete state.
mis.good: The report was incomplete / was in an incomplete state.
mis.why: Say "the report was incomplete" directly without "in".

def: Not staying the same throughout in quality, standards, or character.
ex: Her inconsistent performance on coding challenges made the hiring committee hesitate to make an offer.
nat: The witness gave statements that were completely inconsistent with physical video evidence.

mis.bad: His answers are inconsistent to what he said.
mis.good: His answers are inconsistent with what he said.
mis.why: Always use "inconsistent with", not "inconsistent to".

def: Causing trouble, difficulties, or discomfort.
ex: Scheduling a global team conference call at midnight was extremely inconvenient for Asian members.
nat: Having the nearest grocery store three miles away proved rather inconvenient during winter.

mis.bad: It is inconvenient for me go there.
mis.good: It is inconvenient for me to go there.
mis.why: Remember the infinitive marker "to": "inconvenient for me to go".

def: To include something as part of a whole, or form a legal corporation.
ex: Product managers decided to incorporate user feedback directly into the next sprint cycle.
nat: The new vehicle design incorporates lightweight carbon fiber materials to maximize fuel efficiency.

mis.bad: We incorporated about the suggestions into our work.
mis.good: We incorporated the suggestions into our work.
mis.why: "Incorporate" is transitive and does not take "about".

def: Impossible or very difficult to believe, or extraordinarily good.
ex: The startup achieved incredible growth during its first year, expanding into twelve foreign markets.
nat: From the mountain peak, hikers enjoyed an incredible panoramic view of the ocean.

mis.bad: I had an incredible time with me.
mis.good: I had an incredible time by myself / on my own.
mis.why: Collocate "have an incredible time" naturally without "with me".

def: Not justifiable by argument; unable to be defended against attack or criticism.
ex: The company's decision to dump toxic chemical waste into the river was utterly indefensible.
nat: Leaving sensitive customer passwords unencrypted in plain text files is completely indefensible in engineering.

mis.bad: His behavior was indefensible of justification.
mis.good: His behavior was indefensible / without justification.
mis.why: Use "indefensible" on its own; avoid "indefensible of".

def: Lasting for an unknown or unstated length of time.
ex: The airline announced an indefinite suspension of all direct international flights until repairs finish.
nat: Striking subway transit workers decided to continue their walkout for an indefinite period.

mis.bad: They put the meeting on an indefinite.
mis.good: They postponed the meeting indefinitely / for an indefinite period.
mis.why: "Indefinite" is an adjective, not a standalone noun here; use "indefinitely".

def: The fact or state of being independent and self-governing.
ex: Working remotely for several years gave Sofia immense personal independence and schedule flexibility.
nat: The former colony celebrated its fiftieth anniversary of national independence with vibrant parades.

mis.bad: He wants independence from his parents money.
mis.good: He wants independence from his parents / financial independence.
mis.why: Use "independence from [someone]" or "financial independence".

def: Having no particular interest or sympathy; unconcerned.
ex: The customer support representative seemed totally indifferent to our urgent plea for technical assistance.
nat: Investors remained indifferent to the flashy demo until reliable revenue figures were shared.

mis.bad: He was indifferent with the outcome.
mis.good: He was indifferent to the outcome.
mis.why: Always use "indifferent to", never "indifferent with".

def: Feeling or showing anger or annoyance at what is perceived as unfair treatment.
ex: Local residents grew indignant when town officials raised property taxes without holding hearings.
nat: She gave an indignant reply when colleagues questioned her academic integrity without cause.

mis.bad: He felt indignant with the decision.
mis.good: He felt indignant about / at the decision.
mis.why: Say "indignant at / about something", not "with something".

def: Absolutely necessary; essentially needed.
ex: Reliable high-speed broadband internet has become indispensable for software developers working remotely.
nat: A good pair of supportive walking shoes is indispensable when visiting Rome on foot.

mis.bad: This dictionary is indispensable for me study.
mis.good: This dictionary is indispensable for my studies / for studying.
mis.why: Use "indispensable to [someone]" or "indispensable for [activity/noun]".

def: To allow oneself to enjoy the pleasure of something, or satisfy a desire.
ex: After working tirelessly on the launch, the engineering team indulged in artisan pizza.
nat: Grandparents sometimes indulge their young grandchildren with too many sugary sweets and toys.

mis.bad: I indulged myself with read all night.
mis.good: I indulged myself by reading all night / indulged in reading.
mis.why: Use "indulge in + noun/-ing", not "indulge with + base verb".

def: Not suitable for eating; unfit for human consumption.
ex: The grilled steak was so burnt and dry that it was practically inedible.
nat: Certain wild mushrooms produce potent toxins that make them strictly inedible and lethal.

mis.bad: The soup was very uneatable and inedible to me.
mis.good: The soup was inedible.
mis.why: Use "inedible" directly as a predicate adjective without repeating synonyms.

def: Not producing any significant or desired effect.
ex: The marketing campaign proved completely ineffective at attracting signups from younger tech workers.
nat: Taking expired antibiotic tablets is often ineffective and can encourage dangerous bacterial resistance.

mis.bad: His approach was ineffective to solve the problem.
mis.good: His approach was ineffective in solving the problem / at solving.
mis.why: Say "ineffective in/at solving", not "ineffective to solve".

def: Not achieving maximum productivity; wasting or failing to save time, energy, or money.
ex: Using nested loops over massive arrays can make the script terribly slow and inefficient.
nat: Old heating units are notorious for being inefficient and wasting expensive household electricity.

mis.bad: This algorithm is inefficient in time.
mis.good: This algorithm is computationally inefficient / inefficient in terms of time.
mis.why: Say "inefficient in terms of time" or "computationally inefficient".

def: Having little knowledge or experience in a particular field or activity.
ex: An inexperienced developer accidentally committed sensitive database credentials into the public repository.
nat: The hiring manager gave the inexperienced graduate an internship to foster local talent.

mis.bad: She is inexperienced with to write contracts.
mis.good: She is inexperienced in writing contracts.
mis.why: Use "inexperienced in + -ing/noun", not "with to write".

def: Well known for some bad quality or deed.
ex: The pirate captain became infamous throughout the Caribbean for raiding merchant treasure ships.
nat: That downtown intersection is infamous among local drivers for dangerous rush-hour collisions.

mis.bad: The restaurant is infamous for its delicious pasta.
mis.good: The restaurant is famous for its delicious pasta.
mis.why: "Infamous" has a negative meaning (notorious); for positive fame use "famous" or "renowned".

def: To contaminate with a disease-producing organism or virus, or corrupt something.
ex: Malicious email attachments can infect corporate desktop computers if users open unknown files.
nat: Stagnant floodwaters can quickly infect open wounds with dangerous airborne and waterborne bacteria.

mis.bad: The virus infected to my computer.
mis.good: The virus infected my computer.
mis.why: "Infect" is a transitive verb; do not add the preposition "to".

def: Likely to spread or infect others, or spreading easily as an emotion.
ex: Her energetic laugh and positive attitude were completely infectious across the entire office.
nat: Doctors isolated the patient immediately to stop the spread of the infectious virus.

mis.bad: The disease is very infectious to catch.
mis.good: The disease is highly infectious / easily caught.
mis.why: Avoid adding redundant infinitives like "to catch" after "infectious".

def: Lower in rank, status, or quality.
ex: Using inferior building materials caused the concrete balcony to develop visible cracks rapidly.
nat: Nobody on the team should ever be made to feel inferior or excluded.

mis.bad: This plastic is inferior than metal.
mis.good: This plastic is inferior to metal.
mis.why: Always use "inferior to", never "inferior than".

def: To cause something unpleasant or painful to be suffered by someone or something.
ex: The severe hurricane inflicted catastrophic wind and water damage on coastal residential neighborhoods.
nat: The team was determined not to let the defeat inflict permanent emotional harm.

mis.bad: He inflicted to me a lot of pain.
mis.good: He inflicted a lot of pain on me.
mis.why: Use the pattern "inflict [harm] on / upon [someone]".

def: To fill, pervade, or soak tea or herbs in liquid to extract flavor.
ex: The new creative director managed to infuse fresh energy and optimism into team projects.
nat: Let the chamomile flowers infuse in hot boiling water for about five minutes.

mis.bad: She infused about ideas into the proposal.
mis.good: She infused ideas into the proposal.
mis.why: "Infuse" takes a direct object: "infuse [quality] into [something]".

def: Clever, original, and inventive.
ex: The software architect devised an ingenious caching mechanism that cut response latency in half.
nat: Campers built an ingenious water filtration unit using sand, charcoal, and plastic bottles.

mis.bad: He is very ingenious at speaking English.
mis.good: He is very ingenious / clever with words.
mis.why: Do not confuse "ingenious" (clever/inventive) with "ingenuous" (naive/candid).

def: To take food, drink, or another substance into the body by swallowing or absorbing it.
ex: Young children should never ingest wild berries discovered along forest walking trails unattended.
nat: Certain sea turtles accidentally ingest discarded plastic bags, mistaking them for floating jellyfish.

mis.bad: He ingested of the medicine.
mis.good: He ingested the medicine.
mis.why: "Ingest" is transitive; do not insert the preposition "of".

def: To breathe in air, gas, smoke, or vapor.
ex: Firefighters wear protective oxygen masks so they do not inhale toxic burning fumes.
nat: During the meditation class, participants were told to inhale slowly through the nose.

mis.bad: He inhaled up the fresh mountain air.
mis.good: He inhaled the fresh mountain air deeply.
mis.why: Do not add "up" after "inhale"; use an adverb like "deeply".

def: A person confined to an institution such as a prison or hospital.
ex: The federal prison offers vocational training programs to help inmates find work after release.
nat: Each new inmate is assigned a small cell and basic daily personal items.

mis.bad: He lives in an apartment with his inmate.
mis.good: He lives in an apartment with his roommate.
mis.why: "Inmate" refers to a prisoner or asylum resident, not a flatmate or roommate.

def: A place for the confinement of people accused or convicted of a crime.
ex: The reckless driver spent twenty-four hours in local jail after being arrested for speeding.
nat: He was released from jail after paying the bail amount set by the judge.

mis.bad: He was sent to the jail.
mis.good: He was sent to jail.
mis.why: Omit the definite article "the" when speaking generally: say "sent to jail".

def: A sweet spread made from fruit, or an awkward situation or crowded traffic.
ex: We got stuck in a massive morning traffic jam on the interstate highway for hours.
nat: I spread homemade strawberry jam over freshly toasted whole-wheat bread every morning.

mis.bad: We were blocked in a car jam.
mis.good: We were stuck in a traffic jam.
mis.why: Use "traffic jam", not "car jam".

def: Special words or expressions that are used by a particular profession and are difficult for others to understand.
ex: The doctor avoided medical jargon and clearly explained the diagnosis in simple everyday terms.
nat: Software engineering discussions often contain incomprehensible acronyms and heavy technical jargon.

mis.bad: He used many technical jargons.
mis.good: He used a lot of technical jargon.
mis.why: "Jargon" is uncountable; use "a lot of jargon" or "jargon terms", never "jargons".

def: Each of the upper and lower bony structures in vertebrates forming the framework of the mouth.
ex: The boxer suffered a severe jaw injury during the fifth round of the championship bout.
nat: Chewing tough dried meat can quickly fatigue the muscles around your lower jaw.

mis.bad: His chin hurt after the punch in his jaw.
mis.good: His jaw was fractured in the fight.
mis.why: "Jaw" refers to the bone structure of the mouth, while "chin" is just the bottom point of the face.

def: The state or feeling of being jealous of someone's success or relationships.
ex: Unchecked professional jealousy can quickly destroy trust and collaboration within a high-performing engineering team.
nat: She felt a sudden pang of jealousy when her peer received the promotion.

mis.bad: He feels jealousy about his brother.
mis.good: He feels jealousy toward his brother / is jealous of his brother.
mis.why: Use "jealousy toward [someone]" or the adjective "jealous of".

def: To put someone or something into a situation in which there is a danger of loss, harm, or failure.
ex: Skipping proper data validation could jeopardize the security of millions of user payment profiles.
nat: Arriving late to crucial investor meetings can jeopardize our funding chances this semester.

mis.bad: His actions jeopardized to his career.
mis.good: His actions jeopardized his career.
mis.why: "Jeopardize" is a transitive verb; omit the preposition "to".

def: Danger of loss, harm, or failure.
ex: The sudden cancellation of government funding placed hundreds of research scholarships in serious jeopardy.
nat: One careless tweet placed the diplomat's fragile peace negotiations in double jeopardy.

mis.bad: The company is on jeopardy.
mis.good: The company is in jeopardy.
mis.why: Always use the preposition "in": "in jeopardy", never "on jeopardy".

def: To move or cause to move with a quick, sharp, sudden movement.
ex: The subway train jerked violently forward, causing several standing passengers to lose their balance.
nat: She jerked her hand away from the hot stove burner immediately before getting burned.

mis.bad: The car jerked to forward.
mis.good: The car jerked forward.
mis.why: Do not use "to" with direction adverbs: "jerked forward".

pt: fadiga por fuso horário / jet lag
def: Extreme tiredness and other physical effects felt by a person after a long flight across time zones.
ex: Drinking plenty of water and walking outside helps travelers recover from severe international jetlag.
nat: I experienced brutal jetlag for three full days after flying home from Tokyo.

mis.bad: I am having jetlag.
mis.good: I have jetlag / I am suffering from jetlag.
mis.why: Say "I have jetlag" or "I am suffering from jetlag", not "having jetlag".

def: A short slogan, verse, or tune designed to be easily remembered, or a light ringing sound.
ex: The catchy advertising jingle was stuck in my head for the entire afternoon yesterday.
nat: You could hear the faint jingle of house keys inside his jacket pocket.

mis.bad: The company created a new jingle song.
mis.good: The company created a new commercial jingle.
mis.why: A "jingle" is already a promotional tune; avoid redundant phrases like "jingle song".

def: To link, connect, or become a member or employee of an organization or group.
ex: Several talented international engineers will join our development squad in the upcoming quarter.
nat: Would you like to join us for a quick coffee break after this call?

mis.bad: She joined to the marketing team.
mis.good: She joined the marketing team.
mis.why: "Join" is transitive; do not say "joined to the team".

def: Shared, held, or made by two or more people, parties, or organizations together.
ex: The two tech giants published a joint statement announcing open-source artificial intelligence safety standards.
nat: Couples often open a joint bank account to handle recurring monthly household utility bills.

mis.bad: They made a join effort.
mis.good: They made a joint effort.
mis.why: Use the adjective form "joint", not the verb form "join".

def: An abrupt rough or violent movement, or a surprise shock.
ex: A sudden jolt of electricity surged through the wire when he flipped the breaker.
nat: Reading the bad news gave the executive team a sharp jolt of harsh reality.

mis.bad: The news gave me a big jolt in my heart.
mis.good: The news gave me a sharp jolt.
mis.why: Say "a sharp jolt" rather than overly literal translations.

def: Full of happiness and joy; causing or displaying intense happiness.
ex: The whole village gathered for a joyous celebration after the local team won first place.
nat: Welcoming a healthy newborn baby into the family is always an intensely joyous occasion.

mis.bad: We had a joyous on the wedding.
mis.good: We had a joyous time at the wedding.
mis.why: Use "joyous" as an adjective modifying a noun like "time" or "occasion".

def: A special anniversary of an event, especially one celebrating twenty-five or fifty years.
ex: Citizens lined the streets waving colorful flags to celebrate the monarch's historic golden jubilee.
nat: The university announced several special public lectures to commemorate its diamond jubilee year.

mis.bad: They celebrated the jubilee of company.
mis.good: They celebrated the company's golden jubilee.
mis.why: Use a possessive or descriptive form: "the company's jubilee".

def: Relating to the administration of justice or the function of a judge.
ex: The controversial constitutional reform faced immediate judicial review by the country's highest court.
nat: Judicial independence is a cornerstone principle of any transparent and fair democratic system.

mis.bad: The judge made a very judiciary decision.
mis.good: The judge made a judicial decision.
mis.why: Use "judicial" as the adjective describing actions or systems of courts.

def: The judicial authorities of a country; the branch of government responsible for interpreting laws.
ex: The national constitution clearly separates powers between the executive, the legislature, and the judiciary.
nat: Public confidence in the integrity of the federal judiciary remains essential for social stability.

mis.bad: The judiciary decided to approve the law.
mis.good: The judiciary ruled on the law / The court decided.
mis.why: Remember "the judiciary" is the collective branch; specific verdicts come from "the court".

def: A point where two or more roads, railway lines, or rivers meet.
ex: Turn sharp left at the railway junction and follow signs toward the international airport.
nat: Traffic police installed a new pedestrian crossing at the hazardous suburban highway junction.

mis.bad: Wait for me in the road junction.
mis.good: Wait for me at the road junction.
mis.why: Use the preposition "at" for specific intersections: "at the junction".

def: A particular point in events or time, especially a critical one.
ex: At this critical juncture in the project, we cannot afford any further scope changes.
nat: The ceasefire talks reached a delicate juncture after several border skirmishes were reported.

mis.bad: At this juncture of time, we must decide.
mis.good: At this juncture, we must decide.
mis.why: Avoid adding "of time"; the phrase is simply "at this juncture".

def: Denoting or relating to the younger of two people with the same name, or a lower rank.
ex: The tech firm hired five junior software developers to join their frontend infrastructure team.
nat: As a junior associate, she gained invaluable courtroom experience under senior partners.

mis.bad: He is junior than me in the company.
mis.good: He is junior to me in the company.
mis.why: Use "junior to", never "junior than".

def: Having or showing eagerness or enthusiasm, or having sharp senses.
ex: The new marketing intern is keen to learn everything about programmatic advertising campaigns.
nat: Dogs have a remarkably keen sense of smell that helps detect hidden contraband.

mis.bad: I am very keen for travel.
mis.good: I am very keen on traveling / keen to travel.
mis.why: Use "keen on + -ing" or "keen to + verb", not "keen for + base verb".

def: A person who manages, cares for, or keeps something or someone.
ex: The zoo keeper fed the endangered Bengal tigers their meat early every Tuesday morning.
nat: That clever reusable coffee mug is definitely a keeper for all your morning commutes.

mis.bad: He is the soccer keeper of the team.
mis.good: He is the goalkeeper / keeper for the team.
mis.why: In football (soccer), use "goalkeeper" or "keeper for the team".

def: A small item kept in memory of the person who gave it or in memory of an event.
ex: She kept her grandmother's silver necklace in a velvet jewelry box as a cherished keepsake.
nat: He bought a carved wooden turtle from the artisan market as a travel keepsake.

mis.bad: I bought a keepsake for remember the trip.
mis.good: I bought a keepsake to remember the trip / as a souvenir.
mis.why: Use "to remember" or "as a keepsake", not "for remember".

def: A container or device in which water is boiled, having a lid, spout, and handle.
ex: Fill the electric kettle with cold tap water and press the switch to boil.
nat: The whistle of the metal kettle signaled that the tea water was finally boiling.

mis.bad: I put water in the teapot to boil.
mis.good: I put water in the kettle to boil.
mis.why: A "kettle" boils the water; a "teapot" brews the tea.

def: To take someone away illegally by force, typically to demand a ransom.
ex: Armed criminals tried to kidnap the foreign diplomat on his way home from work.
nat: The movie revolves around detectives attempting to rescue a kidnapped heiress from kidnappers.

mis.bad: They sequestered the businessman.
mis.good: They kidnapped the businessman.
mis.why: Do not use "sequester" (which means isolate or confiscate assets); use "kidnap" for people.

def: A bag with shoulder straps, carried on the back, and typically made of canvas or leather.
ex: The experienced hiker packed waterproof matches, energy bars, and a compass into his canvas knapsack.
nat: She slung the heavy leather knapsack over one shoulder before hurrying to catch the train.

mis.bad: He packed his things in the knapsack bag.
mis.good: He packed his things in his knapsack.
mis.why: A "knapsack" is already a bag; saying "knapsack bag" is redundant.

def: One's family and relations.
ex: The hospital contacted the injured hiker's next of kin before initiating the surgical procedure.
nat: She felt a deep bond with her distant kin living across rural western Canada.

mis.bad: I visited all my kins on Christmas.
mis.good: I visited all my kin / relatives at Christmas.
mis.why: "Kin" is an uncountable collective noun; do not add an "s".

def: To light or set on fire, or arouse or inspire an emotion.
ex: The passionate biology teacher hoped to kindle a genuine love of science among her students.
nat: They gathered dry pine twigs to kindle a small campfire before night fell completely.

mis.bad: The talk kindled in me a passion.
mis.good: The talk kindled a passion in me.
mis.why: "Kindle" takes the direct object first: "kindle [feeling] in [someone]".

def: In a kind, pleasant, or cordial manner; or used in polite requests.
ex: Please kindly verify that your shipping address is up to date before placing orders.
nat: The elderly woman spoke kindly to the nervous child who had lost his way.

mis.bad: He kindly helped me with my luggage.
mis.good: He kindly helped me with my luggage / was kind enough to help.
mis.why: Note: "kindly" can sound stiff in modern casual conversation; "kind" is often simpler.

def: Relating to or resulting from motion.
ex: The falling roller coaster car converts gravitational potential energy into tremendous forward kinetic energy.
nat: The modern art installation uses kinetic sculptures that rotate gracefully in the ambient wind.

mis.bad: The car has a big cinetic energy.
mis.good: The car has a lot of kinetic energy.
mis.why: Spell with a "k" in English: "kinetic", never "cinetic".

def: A country, state, or territory ruled by a king or queen, or a major realm.
ex: The ancient medieval kingdom expanded its borders across the mountains during the eleventh century.
nat: Biologists categorize all living organisms on Earth into major domains and biological kingdoms.

mis.bad: He visited the animal reign.
mis.good: He visited the animal kingdom.
mis.why: Use "kingdom" for natural categories ("animal kingdom") and realms, not "reign" (which is the rule).

def: An acquired or natural skill at performing a task easily and well.
ex: Gabriel has a remarkable knack for debugging tricky memory leaks in multithreaded backend applications.
nat: With a bit of practice, you will quickly develop the knack for making fresh pasta.

mis.bad: She has a knack to learn languages.
mis.good: She has a knack for learning languages.
mis.why: Always say "have a knack for + -ing", not "knack to + base verb".

def: To fall or rest on the knees.
ex: The gardener had to kneel on a soft foam cushion while weeding flower beds.
nat: He knelt down on one knee to propose marriage in front of the fountain.

mis.bad: He kneels down in the floor.
mis.good: He knelt down on the floor.
mis.why: Use "on the floor", not "in the floor", and note the irregular past tense "knelt".

def: To make a garment or fabric by interlocking loops of wool or yarn with needles.
ex: My grandmother loves to knit cozy wool sweaters for all her grandchildren every autumn.
nat: Sharing difficult challenges helped knit the founding team into an exceptionally tight-knit collaborative group.

mis.bad: She likes knitting with needle.
mis.good: She likes to knit / knitting with needles.
mis.why: Use "knitting needles" (plural) when describing the equipment.

def: A rounded lump or ball, especially at the end or on the surface of something.
ex: Turn the temperature adjustment knob clockwise until the indicator light illuminates bright solid green.
nat: He jiggled the brass door knob, but the office door remained firmly locked inside.

mis.bad: He grabbed the door handle knob.
mis.good: He grabbed the doorknob.
mis.why: Combine into "doorknob" or say "door knob", not "handle knob".

def: Heavily loaded or weighed down with something.
ex: The wooden apple trees were laden with sweet red fruit at the end of autumn.
nat: She returned from the busy market laden with fresh organic vegetables and flowers.

mis.bad: The tree was laden of fruit.
mis.good: The tree was laden with fruit.
mis.why: Always use "laden with", never "laden of".

def: To express passionate grief or sorrow, or mourn a loss.
ex: Senior engineers often lament the disappearance of simple and reliable monolithic software architectures.
nat: Citizens gathered outside city hall to lament the loss of historic neighborhood trees.

mis.bad: He lamented about the failed project.
mis.good: He lamented the failed project.
mis.why: "Lament" is transitive; do not insert the preposition "about".

def: A division of a road marked for a single line of vehicles, or a narrow path.
ex: You must switch to the left lane before taking the highway exit ramp toward town.
nat: The cyclist stayed safely inside the designated bicycle lane throughout the city commute.

mis.bad: Change to the other line.
mis.good: Change to the other lane.
mis.why: On a road, use "lane" for traffic lanes, not "line" (which is a queue or boundary mark).

def: To grow weak or feeble, or be neglected in an unpleasant situation.
ex: Unfinished pull requests should not languish in the code review queue for multiple weeks.
nat: The proposed legislation continued to languish in committee without any formal vote.

mis.bad: The project languished of attention.
mis.good: The project languished from a lack of attention.
mis.why: Say "languish from [a cause]" or "languish in [a state]".

def: A brief or temporary failure of concentration, memory, or judgment.
ex: A momentary lapse in concentration caused the tired goalkeeper to allow an easy goal.
nat: The insurance policy was canceled after a two-month lapse in required premium payments.

mis.bad: I had a lapse of memory about your name.
mis.good: I had a temporary lapse of memory.
mis.why: Use "lapse of memory" or "memory lapse" without adding extra prepositions.

def: To a great extent; on the whole; mostly.
ex: The project's rapid success was largely due to excellent team collaboration and disciplined planning.
nat: Her recovery was largely complete within three weeks after the laparoscopic procedure.

mis.bad: The problem was in large part of him.
mis.good: The problem was largely due to his actions.
mis.why: Use the clean adverb "largely due to" rather than awkward translations.

def: Enduring or able to endure over a long period of time.
ex: The mentorship program had a lasting positive impact on the careers of junior designers.
nat: Childhood friendships often create a lasting emotional bond that survives decades of separation.

mis.bad: It left a durable impression on me.
mis.good: It left a lasting impression on me.
mis.why: Collocate with "impression": "lasting impression", not "durable impression".

def: A metal bar with a catch and lever used for fastening a door or gate.
ex: Make sure the heavy front security gate latch clicks firmly shut behind you.
nat: She lifted the wooden latch gently so as not to wake the sleeping child.

mis.bad: The latch of the door was broken.
mis.good: The door latch was broken.
mis.why: Use the compound noun "door latch" for natural English phrasing.

def: Recently; not long ago.
ex: Have you noticed any strange performance degradations on the staging server lately during tests?
nat: I have been sleeping much better lately since starting my evening walking routine.

mis.bad: I have arrived lately to work today.
mis.good: I arrived late to work today / I have been arriving late lately.
mis.why: "Lately" means recently (over time); for tardiness use "late": "arrived late".

def: Existing but not yet developed, manifest, or active; concealed.
ex: The leadership training helped Carlos unlock his latent talent for public speaking and diplomacy.
nat: The virus can remain completely latent inside host cells for several asymptomatic months.

mis.bad: He had a latent of becoming an artist.
mis.good: He had latent talent as an artist.
mis.why: "Latent" is an adjective, not a noun; use "latent talent/ability".

def: Of, at, towards, or from the side or sides, or across hierarchical levels.
ex: She made a lateral career move to the user research team to learn new methodologies.
nat: The physician checked the patient's lateral knee stability following the skiing accident.

mis.bad: He changed to a lateral position of the company.
mis.good: He made a lateral move within the company.
mis.why: The natural idiom for changing jobs at the same pay grade is "lateral move".

def: Deserving praise and commendation.
ex: The startup has a laudable ambition to eliminate all single-use plastic packaging by next year.
nat: Volunteering twenty hours each month at the local food bank is truly laudable work.

mis.bad: His effort was very praiseful.
mis.good: His effort was laudable / praiseworthy.
mis.why: Use "laudable" or "praiseworthy"; avoid inventing words like "praiseful".

def: Sumptuously rich, elaborate, or luxurious, or bestowing something in great quantities.
ex: The entertainment company hosted a lavish launch party at an exclusive rooftop downtown club.
nat: The film critic gave lavish praise to the young director's breakthrough science-fiction debut.

mis.bad: They lived in a lavish life.
mis.good: They led a lavish lifestyle / lived lavishly.
mis.why: Collocate with "lifestyle" ("lavish lifestyle") or use the adverb "lavishly".

def: A sheet, quantity, or thickness of material, typically one of several, covering a surface.
ex: Modern web application security requires multiple defense layers to protect user information effectively.
nat: Wear several light layers of clothing so you can adapt to changing temperatures easily.

mis.bad: The cake has three lines of cream.
mis.good: The cake has three layers of cream.
mis.why: In Portuguese "camada" translates to "layer", never "line".

def: The way in which the parts of something are arranged or laid out.
ex: The graphic designer revised the dashboard layout to make key metrics instantly visible to users.
nat: The open floor layout in the new office encouraged spontaneous conversations across teams.

mis.bad: I changed the disposition of the room.
mis.good: I changed the layout of the room.
mis.why: Do not use "disposition" for physical arrangement; use "layout" or "arrangement".

def: To cause a person or animal to go with one, or be in charge of.
ex: She was chosen to lead the cross-functional engineering project because of her strong communication skills.
nat: Poor communication can easily lead to costly misunderstandings and delayed software project milestones.

mis.bad: This can lead in many problems.
mis.good: This can lead to many problems.
mis.why: Always use "lead to [an outcome]", never "lead in".

def: Culminating in success or holding the foremost position in a field or activity.
ex: She is recognized internationally as a leading expert in pediatric neurological medicine and research.
nat: Our company has become the leading supplier of renewable solar batteries in Latin America.

mis.bad: He is the most leading engineer.
mis.good: He is the leading engineer / one of the leading engineers.
mis.why: "Leading" already implies highest standing; avoid "most leading".

def: To be in or move into a sloping position, or rest against something.
ex: Do not lean against the glass railing on the second-floor balcony while talking.
nat: Companies increasingly lean on cloud automation tools to reduce repetitive manual operational tasks.

mis.bad: He leaned in the wall.
mis.good: He leaned against the wall.
mis.why: Use "lean against the wall" for support, not "in the wall".

def: To jump or spring a long way, to a great height, or with great force.
ex: The agile mountain goat can leap effortlessly across wide rock crevices without falling.
nat: Quarterly earnings leaped thirty percent following the international rollout of the new mobile app.

mis.bad: He leaped over the fence by foot.
mis.good: He leaped over the fence.
mis.why: "Leap" already means jumping on foot; omit redundant phrases like "by foot".

def: Conforming to the law or to rules, or able to be defended with logic.
ex: Customers have a legitimate reason to worry when personal data breaches are not reported promptly.
nat: Always verify that you are downloading software from a legitimate official vendor website.

mis.bad: His complaints are very legitimates.
mis.good: His complaints are legitimate.
mis.why: English adjectives never take plural "-s": say "legitimate", not "legitimates".

def: More merciful or tolerant than expected; not severe.
ex: The traffic police officer was lenient and gave the speeding driver only a warning.
nat: Some professors are quite lenient regarding essay deadlines during intense mid-term exam weeks.

mis.bad: The judge was lenient with to him.
mis.good: The judge was lenient with him / lenient toward him.
mis.why: Use "lenient with / toward [someone]", not "with to".

def: To make or become less; diminish.
ex: Practicing mindfulness exercises each morning can help lessen workplace stress and prevent burnout.
nat: The new bypass road helped lessen heavy commuter traffic through historic downtown streets.

mis.bad: This will diminish the problem to lessen.
mis.good: This will lessen the problem / lessen the impact.
mis.why: Use "lessen" directly as a transitive verb with its object.

def: Sufficient to cause death; harmful or destructive.
ex: The venomous Australian box jellyfish delivers a sting containing potentially lethal biological neurotoxins.
nat: Mixing prescription sleeping pills with alcohol can create an unpredictable and lethal combination.

mis.bad: The poison had a lethal effect of him.
mis.good: The poison had a lethal effect on him.
mis.why: Use "effect on [someone]", not "effect of [someone]".

def: A rigid bar resting on a pivot, used to help move a heavy or firmly fixed load.
ex: Pull the emergency shutoff lever down to immediately cut electricity to the heavy machinery.
nat: Archimedes famously claimed that with a long enough lever, he could move the world.

mis.bad: Push the alavanca to start.
mis.good: Push the lever to start.
mis.why: In Portuguese "alavanca" translates directly to "lever" in English.

def: An act of levying a tax, fee, or fine, or the sum collected.
ex: The municipal government introduced a small congestion levy on cars entering the central district.
nat: Imported luxury electronic devices are subject to an additional federal customs import levy.

mis.bad: The government made a levy over gasoline.
mis.good: The government imposed a levy on gasoline.
mis.why: Use the collocation "impose a levy on [an item]".

def: The state of being responsible for something, especially by law, or a financial debt.
ex: The contract clearly specifies that the vendor accepts full legal liability for data breaches.
nat: His reckless comments during press conferences quickly became a political liability for the campaign.

mis.bad: He has many liabilities on his card.
mis.good: He has substantial liabilities on his balance sheet.
mis.why: "Liability" refers to legal obligations or debts, not simply credit card charges.

def: Responsible by law; legally answerable, or likely to do something.
ex: Property owners are legally liable for injuries that occur on poorly maintained icy sidewalks.
nat: Without proper warm-up exercises, athletes are especially liable to pull tight hamstring muscles.

mis.bad: The tenant is liable about damages.
mis.good: The tenant is liable for damages.
mis.why: Always use "liable for [damages/costs]", not "liable about".

def: Communication or cooperation which facilitates a close working relationship between people or organizations.
ex: Maria was appointed as the technical liaison between our engineering team and executive leadership.
nat: Maintaining close liaison with local law enforcement is essential during major outdoor festivals.

mis.bad: She works in liaison to the client.
mis.good: She acts as a liaison with the client.
mis.why: Use "act as a liaison with [someone]", not "in liaison to".

def: To set someone free from a situation, especially imprisonment or oppression.
ex: Automating repetitive spreadsheets will liberate our team to focus on strategic product development work.
nat: Allied soldiers moved rapidly across northern Europe to liberate occupied cities and villages.

mis.bad: The software liberated us of doing paperwork.
mis.good: The software liberated us from doing paperwork.
mis.why: Always use "liberate from [something]", not "liberate of".

def: The duration of a person's life or the period of something's existence.
ex: Traveling across all seven continents is a dream that takes a lifetime to accomplish.
nat: The company offers a lifetime warranty on all handcrafted solid stainless-steel kitchen cookware.

mis.bad: It was an opportunity of lifetime.
mis.good: It was the opportunity of a lifetime.
mis.why: Always use the full idiom: "the opportunity of a lifetime".

def: To make or become lighter in weight, pressure, or color.
ex: Delegating administrative tasks to junior colleagues helped lighten her intense daily management workload.
nat: The morning sky began to lighten gradually as the sunrise approached the eastern horizon.

mis.bad: We must lighter the burden.
mis.good: We must lighten the burden.
mis.why: Use the verb "lighten", not the comparative adjective "lighter".

def: The fact or quality of being alike; resemblance, or a portrait.
ex: There was an unmistakable physical likeness between the young boy and his great-grandfather.
nat: The artist captured an astonishing likeness of the mayor in the commissioned oil portrait.

mis.bad: He has a likeness with his father.
mis.good: He bears a likeness to his father / resembles his father.
mis.why: Use "bear a likeness to [someone]", not "likeness with".

def: In the same way; also.
ex: The frontend team adopted TypeScript, and the backend engineers decided to do likewise soon.
nat: It was a pleasure meeting you today; likewise, I look forward to working together.

mis.bad: I hope you are well, in the same way, I am good.
mis.good: I hope you are well; likewise, everything is fine here.
mis.why: Use "likewise" as a concise transitional adverb rather than clumsy literal phrasing.

def: An arm or leg of a person or four-legged animal, or a large tree branch.
ex: The gymnast demonstrated exceptional balance and flexible control over every limb during the routine.
nat: A heavy winter snowstorm snapped several large limbs from the ancient oak tree.

mis.bad: He hurt his member during soccer.
mis.good: He hurt his limb / leg during soccer.
mis.why: Do not translate "membro" as "member" for arms and legs; use "limb" or the specific body part.

def: A group of people or things brought together for a particular purpose, event, or team.
ex: The summer music festival announced an impressive lineup of international rock and jazz artists.
nat: The head coach changed the starting lineup after several key players suffered hamstring strains.

mis.bad: The team announced the new escalation.
mis.good: The team announced the new lineup / starting roster.
mis.why: Do not translate Portuguese "escalação" as "escalation"; use "lineup".

def: To stay in a place longer than necessary because of a reluctance to leave.
ex: Guests continued to linger in the warm garden long after the dinner party concluded.
nat: The delicious aroma of freshly baked cinnamon rolls lingered in the bakery for hours.

mis.bad: The smell lingered about the room.
mis.good: The smell lingered in the room.
mis.why: Use "lingered in the room", not "about the room".

def: Relating to language or linguistics.
ex: The researchers conducted an extensive linguistic analysis of medieval Spanish manuscripts found in Toledo.
nat: Living abroad for a full year accelerates your linguistic development through constant natural immersion.

mis.bad: They had problems of idioms.
mis.good: They faced linguistic barriers / language problems.
mis.why: Use "linguistic" or "language" when discussing communication differences.

def: A layer of different material covering the inside surface of something, especially clothing.
ex: The winter coat has a soft quilted fleece lining that keeps you comfortably warm.
nat: Every dark cloud has a silver lining, reminding us that difficult times will pass.

mis.bad: The jacket has a warm liner inside.
mis.good: The jacket has a warm lining inside.
mis.why: Use "lining" for the inner layer of clothing or organs, not "liner".

def: To make or form a connection between two or more things, places, or people.
ex: The newly built suspension bridge will link the island community directly to mainland highways.
nat: Multiple scientific studies link excessive sugar intake directly to increased risk of heart disease.

mis.bad: The studies link sugar with the disease.
mis.good: The studies link sugar to the disease.
mis.why: The standard idiom is "link [something] to [something else]".

def: A substance that flows freely but is of constant volume, having a consistency like water.
ex: Security rules at international airports restrict liquids in carry-on baggage to small bottles.
nat: Drink plenty of clear liquids when recovering from a fever to prevent rapid dehydration.

mis.bad: Do not drink this dangerous fluid liquid.
mis.good: Do not drink this dangerous liquid.
mis.why: Say "liquid"; avoid combining "fluid liquid" redundantly.

def: To wind up the affairs of a business by ascertaining liabilities and converting assets into cash.
ex: The bankrupt retail chain was forced to liquidate its physical inventory at huge discounts.
nat: Investors decided to liquidate their stock holdings before the expected interest rate hike announced.

mis.bad: They liquidated about the company debts.
mis.good: They liquidated the company's debts.
mis.why: "Liquidate" takes a direct object; omit "about".

def: In a literal manner or sense; exactly, without exaggeration.
ex: He translated the foreign expression literally, which made everyone at the table laugh warmly.
nat: There were literally hundreds of applicants competing for the single junior developer position.

mis.bad: I took his words on the literal.
mis.good: I took his words literally.
mis.why: Say "took his words literally", not "on the literal".

def: To resort to legal action to settle a matter.
ex: Both patent holders decided to litigate the dispute in federal court rather than settle.
nat: Litigating complex cross-border intellectual property infringement cases can take five or more years.

mis.bad: They decided to litigate against about the breach.
mis.good: They decided to litigate the dispute in court.
mis.why: Use "litigate [the dispute/claim]" without adding extraneous prepositions.

def: A means of securing the necessities of life.
ex: The prolonged coastal drought threatened the livelihood of thousands of local commercial fishing families.
nat: Many digital creators depend on monthly platform subscription earnings for their everyday livelihood.

mis.bad: Fishing is their principal live.
mis.good: Fishing is their primary source of livelihood / living.
mis.why: Do not use "live" as a noun for income; use "livelihood" or "living".

def: Farm animals regarded as an asset or raised for food, fiber, or labor.
ex: The rural rancher raised various livestock, including cattle, sheep, and free-range dairy goats.
nat: Severe winter blizzards made it difficult to transport hay and feed to isolated livestock.

mis.bad: He bought many livestocks for his farm.
mis.good: He bought a lot of livestock for his farm.
mis.why: "Livestock" is uncountable; never say "livestocks".

def: A heavy or bulky thing that is being carried or is about to be carried.
ex: The electric delivery truck carried a heavy load of wooden shipping crates across town.
nat: Finishing the tax audit took a tremendous load off the small business owner's mind.

mis.bad: I took a weight off my mind.
mis.good: That took a load off my mind.
mis.why: The standard English idiom uses "load": "a load off my mind".

def: To discover the exact place or position of something, or establish in a place.
ex: The rescue search team managed to locate the lost hikers using satellite thermal sensors.
nat: The European logistics company chose to locate its regional distribution headquarters near the port.

mis.bad: I cannot locate where is the file.
mis.good: I cannot locate the file / find where the file is.
mis.why: "Locate" is transitive: "locate the file", or say "find where the file is".

def: A place in which someone lives or stays temporarily.
ex: Our conference registration fee includes daily meals and three nights of hotel lodging accommodation.
nat: Backpackers often search for affordable lodging options like community youth hostels or homestays.

mis.bad: I need to find a cheap hospedage.
mis.good: I need to find affordable lodging / accommodation.
mis.why: Translate Portuguese "hospedagem" as "lodging" or "accommodation", never "hospedage".

def: Of imposing height, or of a noble, elevated, or arrogant nature.
ex: The ambitious clean energy startup set lofty sustainability targets for the upcoming fiscal decade.
nat: Visitors marveled at the cathedral's lofty stone ceilings and stained glass windows above.

mis.bad: He had very high and lofty goals.
mis.good: He had lofty goals for the company.
mis.why: "Lofty" already means very high or elevated; avoid combining with "high".

def: Of or according to the rules of logic or formal argument; clear and sound.
ex: Breaking complex software problems down into smaller modules is always the most logical approach.
nat: There was no logical connection between the customer's complaint and the server error logs.

mis.bad: His explanation was very logic.
mis.good: His explanation was very logical.
mis.why: Use the adjective "logical" to describe reasoning, not the noun "logic".

def: Long life, or long existence or service in a particular position.
ex: Regular cardiovascular exercise, balanced nutrition, and low stress are proven secrets to human longevity.
nat: The extraordinary longevity of the battery system impressed industrial customers around the world.

mis.bad: He had a big longevity of life.
mis.good: He enjoyed remarkable longevity.
mis.why: Avoid saying "longevity of life", which is redundant.

def: A yearning desire or nostalgic affection for something.
ex: After years living in noisy cities, she felt a deep longing for quiet countryside life.
nat: He gazed out the window with an intense longing to travel across the oceans.

mis.bad: I have a longing of my family.
mis.good: I have a longing for my family / I miss my family.
mis.why: Use "longing for [someone/something]", not "longing of".

def: An act of looking something up, especially in an electronic database or index.
ex: Optimizing the database table index reduced the user profile lookup time to under five milliseconds.
nat: A dictionary lookup feature inside the e-reader helps learners understand unfamiliar words instantly.

mis.bad: The function makes a look up on the database.
mis.good: The function performs a database lookup.
mis.why: As a noun, write "lookup" as a single word: "database lookup".

def: A shape produced by a curve that bends round and crosses itself, or a programming iteration.
ex: The developer wrote a simple while loop to process each incoming customer support ticket sequentially.
nat: Keep me in the loop regarding any schedule changes for next week's product demonstration.

mis.bad: Keep me on the loop.
mis.good: Keep me in the loop.
mis.why: The correct idiom is "keep me in the loop", not "on the loop".

def: An ambiguity or inadequacy in the law or a set of rules.
ex: Clever corporate accountants found a legal tax loophole to shelter millions in offshore subsidiary profits.
nat: The government passed emergency legislation to close the regulatory loophole immediately before year-end.

mis.bad: They exploited a breach in the tax law.
mis.good: They exploited a tax loophole.
mis.why: In legal and financial contexts, an ambiguity or oversight in rules is a "loophole", not a "breach".
